notes.summary: Percentage means "out of 100" and is the base of profit and loss, interest, data interpretation and many other topics. SSC asks 1 to 2 direct questions in Tier 1 and 1 to 3 in Tier 2. Learn the fraction table and the successive change formula and most questions take under a minute.

concepts.title: What percent means
concepts.body:
Percent means out of 100. So x% is just the fraction x/100.

  • x% of N = N × x/100. Example: 15% of 240 = 240 × 15/100 = 36.
  • A as a percent of B = A/B × 100. Example: 18 out of 72 is 18/72 × 100 = 25%.
  • x% of y = y% of x. So 8% of 50 = 50% of 8 = 4. Swap when one number is easy.
  • If x% of a number is k, the number is k × 100/x. Example: 30% of a number is 72, so the number is 72 × 100/30 = 240.

To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100: 0.35 = 35%. To change a percent to a decimal, divide by 100: 7.5% = 0.075.

concepts.title: Fraction and percent table (learn by heart)
Increase and decrease as multipliers
concepts.body:
Percentage change = (change / original value) × 100. The base is always the original value.

  • Increase by r%: new = old × (100 + r)/100.
  • Decrease by r%: new = old × (100 − r)/100.

Write the multiplier as a fraction to save time: +25% is × 5/4, −20% is × 4/5, +12.5% is × 9/8, −16 2/3% is × 5/6.

Going back: if the value after a 25% rise is 600, the original is 600 × 4/5 = 480 (not 600 minus 25% of 600).

Example: 85% of a number added to 75 gives the number. Then 75 is 15% of the number, so the number = 75 × 100/15 = 500.

concepts.title: A is r% more or less than B
concepts.body:
If A is r% more than B, then B is less than A by r/(100 + r) × 100%.

If A is r% less than B, then B is more than A by r/(100 − r) × 100%.

The reason: the difference is the same, but the base changes.

Ratio method: if two numbers are 10% and 25% more than a third number, take the third as 100. The two numbers are 110 and 125, so their ratio is 22 : 25.

concepts.title: Successive percentage change
concepts.body:
Two changes of a% and b% one after another give a net change of a + b + ab/100%. Use a minus sign for a decrease.

  • +20% then −10%: 20 − 10 − 200/100 = 8% increase.
  • +a% then −a% (or the other way): always a loss of a²/100%. So +20% then −20% is a 4% fall.
  • Three or more changes: apply the formula twice, or multiply the multipliers. +10%, +10%, −10% gives 1.1 × 1.1 × 0.9 = 1.089, a 8.9% rise.

Chains of comparison work the same way. If A is 20% more than B and B is 30% more than C, A is 20 + 30 + 6 = 56% more than C.

The order of the changes does not matter for the final result.

concepts.title: Population growth and depreciation
concepts.body:
When a value grows by r% every year on its new value (like compound interest):

  • After n years: P × (1 + r/100)n.
  • n years ago: P ÷ (1 + r/100)n.
  • Depreciation (machine value, falling population): use (1 − r/100)n.
  • Different rates in different years: multiply each year’s multiplier, P × (1 + a/100)(1 + b/100)(1 − c/100).

Example: a town of 10,000 grows 10% a year. After 2 years: 10,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 12,100.

Example: a machine worth ₹50,000 loses 20% of its value each year. After 2 years: 50,000 × 0.8 × 0.8 = ₹32,000.

concepts.title: Price, consumption and expenditure
concepts.body:
Expenditure = Price × Consumption. The same rule works for Revenue = Price × Sales, and Area = Length × Breadth.

  • To keep expenditure the same when price rises by r%, cut consumption by r/(100 + r) × 100%.
  • If price falls by r%, consumption can rise by r/(100 − r) × 100%.
  • General case: new expenditure multiplier = price multiplier × consumption multiplier.

Example: price up 25%. Cut = 25/125 × 100 = 20%.

Example: price down 20% and sales up x%, revenue up 60%. Then 0.8 × (1 + x/100) = 1.6, so x = 100.

concepts.title: Price cut gives extra quantity
concepts.body:
If a fall of r% in price lets a person buy q units more for ₹M, then the money saved is r% of M, and it buys exactly q units at the new price.

  • New (reduced) price per unit = (r% of M) / q.
  • Original price per unit = new price × 100/(100 − r).

Example: a 20% fall in the price of bananas gives 6 more bananas for ₹80. Saving = 20% of 80 = ₹16. New price of one banana = 16/6 = ₹8/3, so a dozen costs ₹32.

For a price rise, the same idea gives fewer units: extra money needed is r% of M at the old price.

concepts.title: Income, expenditure and savings
concepts.body:
Income = Expenditure + Savings. Take the income as 100 to make the sum easy.

  • If a person spends 75%, savings are 25%.
  • When income and expenditure change, find the new savings as new income minus new expenditure, then compare with the old savings.

Example: income 100, spends 80, saves 20. Income up 10% and expenditure up 5%. New income 110, new expenditure 84, savings 26. Savings rise by 6/20 × 100 = 30%.

concepts.title: Elections and votes
concepts.body:
• With two candidates, the winning margin = (winner% − loser%) of the valid votes.
  • If some votes are invalid, first find the valid votes: valid = total × (100 − invalid%)/100.
  • If some voters did not vote, polled votes = enrolled voters × (turnout%)/100.

Example: 20% votes invalid. The winner gets 60% of valid votes and wins by 1,600. Margin is 20% of valid votes, so valid = 8,000 and total = 8,000 × 100/80 = 10,000.

concepts.title: Exams and pass marks
concepts.body:
• Pass marks = pass% of maximum marks.
  • A student who gets x marks and fails by f has pass marks x + f. A student who passes by g has pass marks x − g.
  • Two students: (p₂ − p₁)% of maximum = (marks failed by) + (marks passed by).

Example: pass mark 35%. A student gets 210 marks and fails by 14. Pass marks = 224, so maximum = 224 × 100/35 = 640.

concepts.title: Splitting a total in stages
concepts.body:
Many questions cut a total again and again: some did not appear, then some of those who appeared failed, and so on. Each cut is a percent of the current group, not of the original total. Multiply the fractions that remain.

Example: 5% of students did not appear and 20% of those who appeared failed. The part that passed = 0.95 × 0.8 = 0.76 of all students.

Start with 100 (or a convenient number like 1,000) and walk down the tree. It avoids mistakes about which base to use.

concepts.title: Weighted average of percentages
concepts.body:
When two groups with different percentages are joined, the overall percentage is a weighted average, not a simple average.

Overall % = (n₁ × p₁ + n₂ × p₂) / (n₁ + n₂).

Example: 40 boys pass at 80% and 60 girls pass at 90%. Overall pass % = (40 × 80 + 60 × 90)/100 = 86%.

To find the ratio of the groups from the overall percentage, use alligation: n₁ : n₂ = (p₂ − overall) : (overall − p₁).

concepts.title: Percentage change in area and volume
concepts.body:
• Area depends on two lengths. If every side changes by r%, area changes by 2r + r²/100%.
  • Rectangle with length changed by a% and breadth by b%: area changes by a + b + ab/100%.
  • Volume of a cube or sphere changes by the successive formula used three times: (1 + r/100)3 − 1.
  • Perimeter and circumference change by the same r% as the side or radius.

Example: each side of a square up 10%. Area up 10 + 10 + 1 = 21%.

Example: radius of a sphere up 10%. Volume multiplier = 1.13 = 1.331, so volume up 33.1%.

varieties.name: Percent of a number and basic conversions
varieties.how: Write each percent as a fraction, form one equation, and simplify. For "what percent of B is A", find A/B × 100.

example.q: If 20% of (A + B) = 30% of (A − B), then what percentage of B is equal to A?

varieties.name: Percent more or less than
varieties.how: If A is r% less than B, B is r/(100 − r) × 100% more than A. If A is r% more, B is r/(100 + r) × 100% less. For ratios, take the common base as 100.

example.q: Sam’s marks are 19% less than Peter’s. Peter’s marks are how much percent more than Sam’s (correct to two decimal places)?

varieties.name: Successive percentage change
varieties.how: Net change = a + b + ab/100 (minus sign for a fall). For three changes, use it twice or multiply the multipliers.

example.q: The weight of A is 20% more than that of B, and B’s weight is 30% more than C’s. By what percent is A’s weight more than C’s?

varieties.name: Population growth and depreciation
varieties.how: Multiply the year-wise multipliers going forward; divide by them going back.

example.q: The population of a city rose 30% in the first year and fell 15% in the next year. If the present population is 11,050, what was it 2 years ago?

varieties.name: Price, consumption and expenditure
varieties.how: Expenditure multiplier = price multiplier × consumption multiplier. Solve for the unknown multiplier.

example.q: The price of sugar rises by 20%. A person wants his expenditure on sugar to rise by only 8%. By what percent should he cut his consumption?

varieties.name: Price cut lets you buy more
varieties.how: Money saved = r% of the total money. Reduced price per unit = money saved ÷ extra units.

example.q: A 15% fall in the price of salt lets a person buy 2 kg more for ₹272. What is the reduced price per kg?
steps: This buys 2 kg at the new price

varieties.name: Income, expenditure and savings
varieties.how: Take income as 100. Find expenditure and savings before and after, then compare.

example.q: A man spends 80% of his income. His income rises by 20% and his expenditure rises by 15%. By what percent do his savings rise?

varieties.name: Elections and votes
varieties.how: Margin = (winner% − loser%) of valid votes. Remove invalid votes first if they are mentioned.

example.q: In an election between two candidates, one got 64% of the votes and won by 434 votes. How many votes were polled?

varieties.name: Exam marks and pass marks
varieties.how: Pass marks = score + marks failed by = score − marks passed by. With two students, the gap in their percentages equals the sum of the two gaps in marks.

example.q: Anita scored 31% and failed by 16 marks. Sunita scored 40% and got 56 marks more than the pass marks. Find the pass marks.

varieties.name: Splitting a total in stages
varieties.how: Each cut is a percent of the group left at that stage. Multiply the parts that remain and compare with the known number.

example.q: In a school, 4% of the students did not appear in the exam. Of those who appeared, 10% failed. If 1,728 students passed, how many students are in the school?

varieties.name: Weighted average of percentages
varieties.how: Overall % = (n₁p₁ + n₂p₂)/(n₁ + n₂). Use alligation to go the other way.

example.q: In a class, the ratio of rural to urban students is 4 : 7. The average marks of rural and urban students are 65% and 63%. What is the overall average percentage?

varieties.name: Percentage change in area and volume
varieties.how: Area: use the successive formula with the two length changes. Volume: use it three times, or cube the multiplier.

example.q: The radius of a circular disc is decreased by 10%. What is the percentage decrease in its area?

tips: Learn the fractions from 1/2 to 1/20 as percentages. Most options are built from them.
When nothing is given, take the starting value as 100. It turns percents into plain numbers.
Use multipliers: a 25% rise is × 5/4 and a 20% fall is × 4/5. Going back means dividing by the same multiplier.
For any "product" situation (price × quantity, length × breadth, speed × time), use the successive change formula a + b + ab/100.
In two-candidate elections, the margin is the difference of the two percentages of valid votes.
Check the options before solving. A rough answer often picks out the right one.
traps: A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall is not zero change. It is a 4% fall.
"What percent of A is B" uses A as the base: B/A × 100. Read which number is the base.
If A is 25% more than B, B is 20% less than A, not 25%.
In election questions with invalid votes, the candidates’ percentages are usually of valid votes, not of all votes.
Going back from a final value: divide by the multiplier. Do not subtract the percent of the final value.

questions.q: The price of a shirt is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. The net change is:
The population of a town is 10,000. It increases by 10% every year. What will be the population after 2 years?
The price of sugar rises by 25%. By how much percent must a family reduce its consumption so that its expenditure on sugar remains the same?
In an election between two candidates, one candidate gets 58% of the valid votes and wins by 1120 votes. What is the total number of valid votes?
questions.solution:
Loser gets 100 − 58 = 42%.
Margin = 58% − 42% = 16% of valid votes = 1120.
Valid votes = 1120 × 100/16 = 7000.
